newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD leadership will decide on top candidate.
newsitem.headline: German SPD leadership will decide on top candidate.

text.p: Oskar Lafontaine, the leader of Germany's opposition Social Democrats, said the SPD leadership and not he alone would decide who should challenge Chancellor Helmut Kohl next year, a newspaper reported on Friday.

The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung daily said Lafontaine, in an interview with the paper, had gone against an often-repeated view that the leader had the first say on who would be the party's candidate for chancellor in elections due in late 1998.
The paper quoted Lafontaine as saying it was the leadership as a whole which would have the first say on the subject.
Lafontaine and his rival Gerhard Schroeder, the more popular premier of Lower Saxony state, are widely seen as the main contenders to be the party's candidate for chancellor.
Lafontaine, who lost heavily to Kohl in the 1990 elections, told the paper he had not yet decided whether he wanted to take on the chancellor again.
Kohl announced earlier this month he would stand for a record fifth term at the head of his centre-right coalition, putting pressure on the SPD to name their candidate quickly.
But Lafontaine told the Frankfurter Allgemeine the SPD would stick to its plan of not deciding until April next year -- after Schroeder has stood for reelection as Lower Saxony premier.
Opinion polls show Schroeder as the voters' favourite prospective chancellor, ahead of both Kohl and Lafontaine.

Germans do not vote directly for a chancellor but for individual parties and regional candidates. Polls show, however, that the candidate a party nominates for chancellor can have a significant impact on its electoral fortunes.
The SPD leadership has been unsettled ever since Kohl manoeuvred Helmut Schmidt out of power in 1982.
The disorientated party broke ground with a U.S.-style primary vote to pick a new chairman, Rudolf Scharping, in 1993. He lost to Kohl in a general election the following year.
